## Build: Your First Quarto Document

In a new `.qmd` file, add a code chunk and some narrative text around it:

```{webr-r}
summary(rawc)
```

Render (knit) the document to see the text and code output combine into 
one finished file.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Learn More — Themes and Output Formats
Changing `format: html` to `format: pdf` or `format: docx` in the YAML 
header changes your entire output type without touching a single line of 
analysis code — the same document can become a slideshow, a PDF, or a Word 
file depending only on this header.
:::

## Create a Quarto Document for Publishing

In this exercise you will create a publication-quality document using a 
PLOS journal template, run a gene variability analysis, and generate a 
heatmap figure.

### Setup

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
# if any are missing: install.packages("tidyverse"); install.packages("readxl"); install.packages("scales")
```

::: callout-tip
## Checking installed packages in Positron
You can also check in the **Extensions** pane by searching for the package name.
:::

### Install the PLOS Template

```bash
quarto add quarto-journals/plos
quarto use template quarto-journals/plos
```

::: callout-note
## What this does
This installs a Quarto extension that formats your document to match PLOS 
journal submission requirements — layout, fonts, and figure formatting. 
The same approach works for other journal templates under `quarto-journals`.
:::

### Gene Variability Analysis

Copy this into your `publication.qmd` under `## Gene Variability Analysis`:

```r
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gene_data_long <- gene_data %>%
  rename(ensembl_id = `...1`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene_symbol), gene_symbol != "") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(ensembl_id, gene_symbol),
               names_to = "sample",
               values_to = "expression")

gene_variability <- gene_data_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol, ensembl_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_expression          = mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance                 = var(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    coefficient_of_variation = sd(expression, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_expression,
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

top_genes <- gene_variability %>%
  arrange(desc(variance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

cat("Total genes analyzed:", nrow(gene_variability), "\n")
cat("Mean variance across all genes:",
    round(mean(gene_variability$variance, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
cat("Most variable gene:", top_genes$gene_symbol[1],
    "with variance =", round(top_genes$variance[1], 2), "\n")

cat("\nTop 10 most variable genes:\n")
print(top_genes %>%
        select(gene_symbol, variance) %>%
        slice_head(n = 10) %>%
        mutate(variance = round(variance, 2)))
```

### Data Visualization

Copy this into your `publication.qmd` under `## Data Visualization`:

```r
#| fig-cap: "Expression heatmap showing scaled expression levels of the
#|   15 most variable genes across all samples. Blue indicates
#|   below-average expression, white indicates average expression,
#|   and red indicates above-average expression for each gene."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

heatmap_data <- gene_data_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_genes$gene_symbol) %>%
  left_join(top_genes %>% select(gene_symbol, variance),
            by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(scaled_expr = scale(expression)[, 1]) %>%
  ungroup()

expression_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample,
             y = reorder(gene_symbol, variance),
             fill = scaled_expr)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
    name = "Scaled\nExpression", limits = c(-3, 3),
    oob = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression Variability Heatmap: Top 15 Most Variable Genes",
    subtitle = "Genes ordered by variance (highest at top)",
    x = "Sample ID", y = "Gene Symbol"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, face = "italic"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# print(expression_heatmap)  # not needed when rendering a full .qmd —
# your rendered document and outputs/ folder will show the result

ggsave(paste0("outputs/", timestamp, "_expression_heatmap.png"),
       plot = expression_heatmap, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

Render your `publication.qmd` document to see your PLOS-formatted article.

::: callout-tip
## Saving your figure
The `ggsave()` call saves a high-resolution `.png` to your `outputs/` 
folder with a timestamp in the filename — the same automated file naming 
pattern introduced in Arc 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 💻 Try It Live — Browser-Based / Async Students

If you don't have R installed locally, you can run this whole analysis 
directly in your browser. `ggsave()` won't actually save a file here, 
since this sandbox has no real file system — so `print()` stays active 
instead, to show you the plot directly on this page.

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(janitor)

gene_data <- rio::import(here::here("raw_data", "GSE113754_GeneLevel_Raw_data.csv")) %>%
  clean_names()

timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

gene_data_long <- gene_data %>%
  rename(ensembl_id = `...1`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene_symbol), gene_symbol != "") %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(ensembl_id, gene_symbol),
               names_to = "sample",
               values_to = "expression")

gene_variability <- gene_data_long %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol, ensembl_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_expression          = mean(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance                 = var(expression, na.rm = TRUE),
    coefficient_of_variation = sd(expression, na.rm = TRUE) / mean_expression,
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

top_genes <- gene_variability %>%
  arrange(desc(variance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

heatmap_data <- gene_data_long %>%
  filter(gene_symbol %in% top_genes$gene_symbol) %>%
  left_join(top_genes %>% select(gene_symbol, variance),
            by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  mutate(scaled_expr = scale(expression)[, 1]) %>%
  ungroup()

expression_heatmap <- heatmap_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample,
             y = reorder(gene_symbol, variance),
             fill = scaled_expr)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
    name = "Scaled\nExpression", limits = c(-3, 3),
    oob = scales::squish
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Expression Variability Heatmap: Top 15 Most Variable Genes",
    subtitle = "Genes ordered by variance (highest at top)",
    x = "Sample ID", y = "Gene Symbol"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, face = "italic"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

print(expression_heatmap)
# ggsave() is commented out here — this browser sandbox has no real
# file system to save to. On your own machine, this line writes a
# real, timestamped .png to your outputs/ folder.
# ggsave(paste0("outputs/", timestamp, "_expression_heatmap.png"),
#        plot = expression_heatmap, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```
:::

---

## What We Did, and Why

**What we built:** converted a plain README into a Quarto document with 
an auto-generated, annotated project tree; then created a separate 
publication-ready document using a real journal template, a gene 
variability analysis, and a saved heatmap figure.

**Why it matters:** your project's own documentation now regenerates 
itself instead of going stale, and your path from raw data to a 
publication figure is a script someone else could re-run — not a series 
of manual steps living only in your memory.
